Truffles - the Mozart of Mushooms

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Truffles, one the most expensive food itmes in the world - now grown in a lab

Unique Selling Point:
A truffle hunting sniffer dog goes crazy and starts to dig in the ground a few feet away from an oak tree in Ceres, Western Cape. He uncovers a round black fungus looking mushroom . Our presenter holds the truffle in his hands – and says that the dig simply cant eat the black truffle , after all, the international market price of truffles is R35 000 a kilogram!

Truffles are one of the most expensive delicacies in the world and have earned many titles -

The black diamond of the kitchen. The Mozart of mushrooms. The jewel of cuisine. These are some of the labels that the truffle has earned for itself over time.

The highly sought after nutty and oniony taste and aroma make Truffles perfect for pastas, eggs, poultry and other dishes!

In this insert about the newly emerging truffle industry in South Africa, we will portray how a South African laboratory in Pretoria is now creating a world first – producing truffles in a laboratory, something thought impossible, till now.

Summary:
Today, truffles are found in temperate areas of Mediterranean Europe, western North America and Australia.

And they are NOW being now grown in South Africa – because we have the ideal climate for it, a Mediterranean climate,but truffle growers here can't keep up with the demand and chefs have to order from abroad.

Just why are they so expensive -

Huge expenses training dogs to become sniffer dogs. Pigs have also been trained to sniff out TRUFFLES that lie below the surface but they tend to eat the truffles so there is a preference to use dogs.
Takes at least a 6 years for truffles to grow, after a plantation has been planted.
There is a short season of about 4 months for a yield.
Truffles have to be taken out of the ground at the exact time or they “go off” so there is a lot of management required.
Once a truffle has been taken from the ground, it has to be cleaned, graded and sold and eaten within 2 or 3 weeks, or they “go off” and can't be used.



Further information:
Enter the guru of Truffles in SA – 80 year old Volker Miros in Cape Town who family company is called Woodford Truffles – in Houtbay and their plantation and lab is in Ceres, Western Cape.

German born Volker Miros's interest in mushrooms started at a very early age when he mushroom hunted with his grandfather in the forests of around Stuttgart, Germany. Later in life, Volker’s interest in food steered him to become a prominent Food Photographer.

 South Africa will come into truffle production he says very soon and will be able to supply the Northern Hemisphere markets thorough the establishment of the Partnerships between Woodford Truffles SA (Pty) Ltd and their selected producers.
This company goes into partnerships with aspirant truffle farmers; In their nursery and laboratory, they infuse an acorn with DNA which creates truffles. . And they grow 100o's of seedlings – when the tree has reached a height of about 18 inches, they then give to aspirant farmers. But first they do scientific tests to make sure that the land used by aspirant farmers is cold enough and has enough lime in the soil. Their sterile environments and DNA certification ensures superior truffles and, thus, higher profit margins.
Vonker and his team show a genuine interest in the laboratory in Pretoria – Dagutat Science company name – who now are cultivating truffles . The scientists involved are Nita Breytenbach and Helga Dagutat.


There are just no pigs or dogs involved and they’re not grown 20cm below the ground. They can be grown to different sizes and are not limited by the seasons. 
Almost unbelievably, they are also growing and have grown the Piedmontese white Alba truffle, the Tuber magnatum. which is the most expensive truffle in the world.
In a laboratory – a world first.
I see an upbeat sometimes humerus insert on the mystery of truffles, we will go on a truffle hunt with a sniffer dog , of how SA is entering the world market – and we throw in a crazy chef as well. We also describe a world first – creating truffles in a lab.

Paul Miros

And that's Volker Miros who set up the truffle lodge on his farm Groenfontein in the southern cedarberg.

Derek: Does that title sit well with you?
Volker: well it took a long time to get to that title I suppose...a lot of studying, and errors, we made on the farm... but I am quite proud of it actually.

Volker grew up in Germany and as a child he loved to forage for mushrooms

Volker: Belitas, pinegreens, asorts of stuff was collected, and put in the family roast, it's a smell that you never forget.

Volker and his family , who escaped to Austria just prior to world war 2, later arrived in cape town after the war. He carved out a successful career as a film maker and food photographer .On assignment in Nambia he photographed the kalahari truffle which grows in the wild - called the nabba.

He spent several years perfecting the science on how to to successfully cultivate truffles( in south africa).. To date he has planted 22 hectares of oaks on his farm all inoculated with the black PERIGOOR winter tuffle spore. Volker\s son Paul, who heads up marketing says that once acorns start germinating in their nurseries, inoculation takes place

Paul: we basically take the truffles that we have imported from Italy, and we mash them up into a liquid, add a secret ingredient, and we put them on the roots, and then we let nature run its course.

Batch checks are performed to determine if the fungus has attached to the roots. Woodford truffles are partnership with a small group of farmers and supplied them with over 625 000 inoculated (truffle producing )saplings.

Gerald: it was just a hobby initially, but then I started to get into it, spending some time with other truffle farmers, then it started to feel more realistic.

Xxxxxxxxxx

Derek: up to now, have you tried one of your home grown truffles?

Gerald: Other farmers but not my own yet, there is a bottle of champaign waiting for that day!!

xxxxxxxxx
GERALD is expecting his first yield next year. Derek: when I told my wife that I was doing a story on truffles, she said oh we have truffle lil in the pantry – and it's cheap!

Paul: Truffle oil is synthetic, it is one of ur biggest problems, people are starting to get so used to that, ut does not taste like the real thing.

we are going to meet some of the most important member if the team, Bonnie and Clyde.

Xxxxxxxxxxxxx 2
Bonnie and Clyde have been trained by Trevor and Marda Norris to find these treasures, .Truffle season in south Africa is in winter so truffles were imported for a demonstration.

Derek: Right now we are going to hide a truffle, there it is, ad my main duty is to make sure that the dogs aren't looking!

About a hundred meters away Paul buried a truffle. ............a well trained dog, like Bonnie, is able to detect the ripening truffle aroma..and then will lead its owner to the jack pot, ….. Any dog that has the capacity for training can be used.

(back in the kitchen) Christof had prepared some truffle dishes for us. He grated about R600's worth of truffles onto these 2 simple pasta dishes... Time to experience the magic.

Derek:...quite delicious...
Christoffe: merci
Derek: otherwise I would say, baie lekker...but very expensive as well, but it's unique!

In the meantime something remarkable is happening in a laboratory in Pretoria at a company called Dagutat, where we received a warm welcome: it's core business is producing biological products for crop protection – but in 2017 a new challenge presented itself to Helga Dagutat and Nita Breytenbach.
XXXXXXXXXX

Helga: when me and Nita went for business in europe, we came across a truffle, snd I said, lets bliksem it, let's try this... it started with the idea, we think in another direction and start growing the truffles..

Derek: Like myth busters..

Helga: laughs

Their truffles grow in moss chambers, but , their methods remain top secret

Derek: what was it like when you produced your first truffle...

.. derek to be honest we have drunk lots of champaign everytime we have our truffles, we have worked very hard to make the chambers productive, as we want to go commercial with the trufles:

To date they have produced 70 truffles including the much sought after white truffle,

Link: so we did not get to hear about the science, or even peek at the equipment, but we are going to taste a lab truffle.



Derek: Def a very attractive, pleasing taste and an aroma – mmmmm.

But.. Christof prefers them to be grown in the traditional way... (or au naturaal)

Derek: So no lab truffles for you:

Chistoffe: no no no no

Helga and Nita say that chefs have applauded their truffles, and when in full production they will be ale to produce around the year...they also don't plan to undercut the current price of truffles.

Meanwhile back at the lodge Volker says that aspirant truffle farmers need to be passionate and have Perseverance.

Volker: and deep pockets,........

Pigs have also been trained to sniff out TRUFFLES that lie below the surface but they tend to eat the truffles so there is a preference to use dogs. Takes at least a 6 years for truffles to grow, after a plantation has been planted. There is a short season of about 4 months for a yield. Truffles have to be taken out of the ground at the exact time or they “go off” so there is a lot of management required. Once a truffle has been taken from the ground, it has to be cleaned, graded and sold and eaten within 2 or 3 weeks, or they “go off” and can't be used.
metadata.Further information: Enter the guru of Truffles in SA – 80 year old Volker Miros in Cape Town who family company is called Woodford Truffles – in Houtbay and their plantation and lab is in Ceres, Western Cape. German born Volker Miros's interest in mushrooms started at a very early age when he mushroom hunted with his grandfather in the forests of around Stuttgart, Germany. Later in life, Volker’s interest in food steered him to become a prominent Food Photographer. South Africa will come into truffle production he says very soon and will be able to supply the Northern Hemisphere markets thorough the establishment of the Partnerships between Woodford Truffles SA (Pty) Ltd and their selected producers. This company goes into partnerships with aspirant truffle farmers; In their nursery and laboratory, they infuse an acorn with DNA which creates truffles. . And they grow 100o's of seedlings – when the tree has reached a height of about 18 inches, they then give to aspirant farmers. But first they do scientific tests to make sure that the land used by aspirant farmers is cold enough and has enough lime in the soil. Their sterile environments and DNA certification ensures superior truffles and, thus, higher profit margins. Vonker and his team show a genuine interest in the laboratory in Pretoria – Dagutat Science company name – who now are cultivating truffles . The scientists involved are Nita Breytenbach and Helga Dagutat. There are just no pigs or dogs involved and they’re not grown 20cm below the ground. They can be grown to different sizes and are not limited by the seasons. Almost unbelievably, they are also growing and have grown the Piedmontese white Alba truffle, the Tuber magnatum. which is the most expensive truffle in the world. In a laboratory – a world first. I see an upbeat sometimes humerus insert on the mystery of truffles, we will go on a truffle hunt with a sniffer dog , of how SA is entering the world market – and we throw in a crazy chef as well. We also describe a world first – creating truffles in a lab.
